title: Who, Which, That
subtitle: Add extra information about a person or thing in the same sentence.
objectives: Use "which" for things, especially with extra, comma-separated information
Use "that" for people or things, without commas

content.intro: Instead of two short sentences ("I have a dog. It loves to play."), you can combine them into one, more natural sentence using who, which, or that.

rules.heading: The basics
rules.body:
• who → people: The man who lives next door is friendly.
  • which → things, often with extra information set off by commas: The book, which you gave me, is very interesting.
  • that → people or things, no commas, common in everyday speech: I have a dog that loves to play fetch.

examples: The man who lives next door is very friendly.
I have a dog that loves to play fetch.
The book, which you gave me, is very interesting.
The teacher who taught us math is retiring.
The car, which she bought last year, is red.
This is the restaurant that we talked about.

commonMistakes.wrong: The man which lives next door is friendly.
commonMistakes.right: The man who lives next door is friendly.
commonMistakes.why: "Which" is for things, not people — use "who" (or "that").

commonMistakes.wrong: I have a dog who loves to play. (informal, less standard)
commonMistakes.right: I have a dog that loves to play. / I have a dog which loves to play.
commonMistakes.why: For animals and things, "that" or "which" is the standard choice, not "who."

commonMistakes.wrong: The book, that you gave me, is interesting.
commonMistakes.right: The book, which you gave me, is interesting.
commonMistakes.why: "That" is never used with commas (extra information) — use "which" instead.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with who, which, or that.

items.prompt: The man ___ lives next door is very friendly.
I have a dog ___ loves to play fetch.
The book, ___ you gave me, is very interesting.
items.explanation: Extra information with commas needs "which," never "that."

items.prompt: The teacher ___ taught us math is retiring.
The car, ___ she bought last year, is red.
items.explanation: Extra, comma-separated information about a thing needs "which."

items.prompt: This is the restaurant ___ we talked about.
items.explanation: "That" is the natural, everyday choice here (no commas, defining information).

items.incorrect: The woman which called you is my sister.
answer: The woman who called you is my sister.
The woman that called you is my sister.
items.explanation: "Which" is only for things, not people.

items.incorrect: My car, that is very old, still works.
answer: My car, which is very old, still works.
items.explanation: "That" is never used with commas — use "which" instead.

summary: Who = people. Which = things, often with commas. That = people or things, no commas.
Never use "that" with commas — use "which" for extra information about a thing.
